doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Practicing in the barn and Tommy Flanagan opening his eyes to jazz
summary: Winter practice in the barn, a piano at about eleven, and meeting Tommy Flanagan at Northern High School.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: No, no, no. They said you want to bang on it? Bang on it out in the barn. And I did, winter and spring and summer and fall I’d go out there. I got so good I used to cut the fingers off my gloves in the wintertime, and put my coat around my neck and go out and play, and practice that piano. I’d get some hours in some days, until I got old enough and started — it seemed like I was going to be serious about it — I was about ten or eleven years old. And then she says okay, you can get a piano. But I had to go through a lot to get a piano. When I was about eleven or twelve, I met Tommy Flanagan in high school. And Tommy was really the first guy to open my eyes to jazz. I had heard jazz, but I didn’t care too much for it up until about eleven years old. And when I heard Tommy play I went right up to him and I said what kind of music are you playing? You don’t have any music in front of you. What are you doing? He said, “Don’t you know about Charlie Parker?” I said, “Bud Powell? Who is Bud Powell?” Finally, because I would sit, after he’d play, I’d sit right down and play a Chopin etude. And he’d say you got all this from this music? So we just exchanged ideas, and it was Tommy who influenced me, really, to play jazz. He said, “Hey, do you know the changes to the blues?” We were at the Northern High School, a long time ago, I hate to think how long ago it was. But no, the church, although it had an influence, it didn’t have a direct influence. It wasn’t until I was a grown man that I began to use elements of Gospel music actually.
